extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate students writing academic research reports, term papers, theses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for planning, drafting, citing, and structuring academic research reports, emphasizing coherence, evidence use, and avoidance of plagiarism. Targets students preparing research papers, theses, or long reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using sources' key terms without original argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If the key terms that run through your report are the same as those in one or more sources, consider whether you are making your own argument or mimicking theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If key terms match source(s), check that you are advancing your own analysis rather than echoing others. Rewrite to clarify your original contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not map report directly onto assignment language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not map your report directly on to the language of your assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid echoing the assignment wording in your opening paragraph — it suggests no original ideas. Rephrase the task into your own problem statement and organizational plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical compare-then-compare organization
rubrics_metrics.description: If your assignment lists a series of issues to cover, avoid addressing them in the order given or organizing into two separate summaries (e.g., Freud then Jung).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break topics into conceptual parts (definitions, elements) and order them usefully for readers so the paper doesn't read as unrelated summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch a working introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a sketchy working introduction to start drafting; expect to write it twice (a working intro for you, a final one for readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final introduction will usually have four parts (see chapter 16). Use the working intro to anticipate those parts and to guide early drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize only key points of most relevant sources
rubrics_metrics.description: At the top of the first storyboard page, sketch a brief summary of only the key points in only those sources most relevant to your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long accounts of marginal references. Summarize only sources you intend to correct, modify, or expand on, and order them in a way useful to readers (chronologically, by significance, point of view). Do not follow the order you read them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrase the question as a statement of a gap or flaw
rubrics_metrics.description: After your summary of sources, rephrase your question as a statement about a flaw or gap you see in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn an assignment question into a concrete research gap (example: 'Few historians have explained why the Alamo story has become so important...'). This frames your point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch an answer to 'So what?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch an answer to 'So what if we don't find out?' to indicate the significance of your research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can't answer it now, skip and return later, but try to articulate why the topic matters (e.g., helps understand national values).

rubrics_metrics.name: State main point early or promise an answer (social contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the answer to your question as your point or promise an answer in a launching point. You may state it at the end of the introduction or only in the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the main point at the end of the introduction lets readers read faster and keeps you on track; waiting until the conclusion creates a more controlling relationship. If you delay, include a launching sentence with key terms to guide readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a concise road map only if appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers add a short road map at the end of the introduction (e.g., 'In part 1... Part 2...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Road maps are common in social sciences but can be clumsy in humanities. If used, keep it short; you may include one on the storyboard to guide drafting and then cut it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify key concepts that run through the whole report
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle four or five words that express the key concepts relevant to your specific question and main point; ignore general topic words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List those key terms at the top of each storyboard page and check their recurrence while drafting. If few key terms appear, your topic may be too general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch background and define necessary terms
rubrics_metrics.description: After the introduction page, add a storyboard page outlining necessary background, definitions, limits, or contextual placement of your problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep background concise and focused on what's necessary for understanding your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a storyboard page for each major section with a clear point
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a page for each major section; at the top write the point that the rest of that section supports, develops, or explains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually the section point is a reason supporting your main claim. Using clear section points helps maintain coherence between parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a reader-centered order for sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a suitable order for sections that meets readers' needs rather than following how the material occurred to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering options: part-by-part, chronological, short-to-long/simple-to-complex, more familiar-to-less familiar, less contestable-to-more contestable, more important-to-less important (or vice versa), earlier understanding to prepare for later, general analysis followed by specific applications. Make the principle of order clear on storyboard pages (e.g., 'First...', 'More important...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight section-unique key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: At the top of each section/storyboard page, circle the key terms that uniquely distinguish that section from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot find distinguishing terms, reassess the section's contribution; it may offer little and could be cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate where to put evidence, acknowledgments, warrants, summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: On each section storyboard page, indicate placement for evidence, acknowledgments/responses, warrants, and summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts may need their own sub-arguments; planning placement helps structure each section logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group and explain evidence clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sections consist of evidence supporting a reason; group different kinds of evidence and note where to explain origin, reliability, and exactly how they support the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order evidence so it makes sense to readers; flag where an explanation of evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate objections and outline responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine what readers might object to and outline a response; responses may be full sub-arguments with claims, reasons, evidence, and further responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including acknowledgments and responses strengthens your argument and preempts reader doubts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State warrants when needed and support them if questioned
rubrics_metrics.description: If readers might not accept the link between reason and claim, state the warrant before offering the claim and support the warrant if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make implicit assumptions explicit for non-expert readers. If a warrant is contestable, provide evidence or argument for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize progress at ends of long/fact-heavy sections
rubrics_metrics.description: If your report is long and fact-heavy, consider ending each major section with a brief summary of what has been established and how the argument stands so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interim summaries aid reader comprehension; delete them later if they seem clumsy in the final draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch a working conclusion with significance
rubrics_metrics.description: State your point again at the top of a conclusion storyboard page and, if possible, sketch its significance (another answer to 'So what?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conclusion page to crystallize your argument and its implications; refine it in final revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start drafting early and accept imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Start drafting as soon as you can; avoid waiting for a perfect report that will never exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft early to discover ideas. Aim for the best you can in the time available, then revise; accept that final work is a tested, supported 'truth' within limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft in a way that fits your working style
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft in a way that feels comfortable: some writers draft early and explore, others need a meticulous plan and proceed slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick drafters let words flow, omit details to fill later, and need time to revise; slow drafters require a detailed outline. Most work best drafting quickly then revising carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use key words and headings to stay on track
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your key concepts in front of you and check how often you use them; use headings while drafting even if your field usually doesn't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create headings from the words unique to a section to show structure at a glance; remove them in the final draft if inappropriate to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize, paraphrase, or quote appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide case-by-case: summarize when details are irrelevant; paraphrase when you can state a source more clearly or your argument depends on details but not exact words; quote for specific evidentiary or rhetorical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote when words themselves are evidence, when an authority's words back a claim, when wording is strikingly original, or when you fairly state a view you disagree with. Always cite bibliographic data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate quotations correctly (run-in vs block and three integration methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signal direct quotations as run-ins for four or fewer quoted lines (surrounded by quotation marks) and as indented blocks for five or more lines. Insert quotations by dropping them in with identifying words, introducing them with an interpretive sentence, or weaving their grammar into your sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the integration style that clarifies the quotation's role. Use identifying phrases (Author says...), interpretive lead-ins, or grammatical weaving to make quotations part of your prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify quotations only with proper signals
rubrics_metrics.description: You may modify quotations so long as you don't change meaning; signal deletions with ellipses and changes with square brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure modifications preserve original intent; examples show how to fit quotations grammatically into your sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how evidence supports your claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce complex evidence with a sentence stating what you want readers to get out of it; evidence does not speak for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before presenting long quotations or data sets, tell readers why it's relevant and how it supports your reason (example with Hamlet passage). Apply the same to tables and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against inadvertent plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid practices that make readers think you are passing off others' work as your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risky behaviors include: quoting/paraphrasing/summarizing without citation; using ideas or methods without citation; citing but failing to use quotation marks for exact words; paraphrasing so closely that wording remains essentially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the source of every quotation, paraphrase, or summary
rubrics_metrics.description: You must cite your source every time you use its words, even if you paraphrase or summarize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material comes from different pages cite each one; if a paraphrase spans several paragraphs cite once at the end. Add citations immediately when you insert quotations to avoid losing track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal every quotation even when cited
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you cite the source, readers must know which words are not yours by using quotation marks or block quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some short phrases may not require marks if not original, but striking phrases do. When in doubt, use quotation marks; follow disciplinary norms (e.g., lawyers may quote statutes without marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't paraphrase too closely
rubrics_metrics.description: A paraphrase becomes plagiarism when readers can match your words and phrasing with those of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To paraphrase safely: read the passage, look away, think, paraphrase from memory, then check for too-close similarity (word-for-word parallels). Revise if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite ideas that are associated with a person or are not common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually cite a source for ideas not your own when the idea is associated with a specific person and is new enough not part of common knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need to cite widely known facts (e.g., 'the world is round'), but you should cite recent or attributable scholarly claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not plead ignorance or innocent intent to avoid citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of free web availability or innocent misunderstanding do not exempt you from citing borrowed material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author would recognize her words or ideas in your paper, cite and quote appropriately. Teachers judge words, not intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations have social and rhetorical importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct citations protect you from plagiarism charges and contribute to your ethos, help readers evaluate and follow your work, and honor sources by acknowledging intellectual debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate citations show attention to detail and reliability; readers preview sources to assess trustworthiness; citations sustain scholarly community norms and credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow appropriate citation style precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure to use the citation style required by your field (two basic patterns: author-title and author-date) and follow its prescriptions down to commas and spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-title (title follows author) is common in humanities (Chicago/Turabian, MLA). Author-date (date follows author) is common in sciences/social sciences (Chicago/Turabian author-date, APA). Use style manuals or reliable online guides; check with instructor about citation software use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work through procrastination and writer's block with concrete strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can't start or write, diagnose causes and use targeted remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes/remedies: break the task into small steps; set achievable goals and routines; use progress charts or writing partners; avoid perfectionism by writing informally early; seek counseling for severe anxiety; sometimes let ideas simmer by stepping away briefly.
